sentences.text: Prosaurolophus is defined by a small, solid crest made of nasal bones positioned just in front of the eyes.
This most important feature consists of nasal bones projecting upward in front of the eye sockets.
As a hadrosaurine duck-billed dinosaur, it is distinguished by lacking a hollow crest.
The most complete described specimen possessed a skull approximately 90 centimeters long and a total body length of 8.5 meters.
The largest known individual measured 8.5 meters in length and weighed 3 metric tons.
Charles Sternberg observed that a 'hocked' ischium once assigned to Saurolophus was not actually found with the holotype.
William Parks later discovered a complete Prosaurolophus skeleton in 1924 that showed a 'bare' ischium.
Earlier genera previously grouped with Prosaurolophus were later reclassified into Stephanosaurinae or Hadrosaurinae.
The type species Prosaurolophus maximus was formally described by Barnum Brown in 1916.
Barnum Brown unearthed a skull in 1915 for the American Museum of Natural History, cataloged as AMNH 5836, from the Red Deer River in Alberta near Steveville.
A second species, Prosaurolophus blackfeetensis, was described by Jack Horner in 1992.
Prosaurolophus was a large herbivore with a sophisticated skull capable of mastication-like plant processing.
Prosaurolophus maximus likely acted as a browser, feeding on conifer trees and bark in coastal floodplains rather than grazing.
Like most hadrosaurs, Prosaurolophus had a flat front of the skull that widened rostrally to form a beak ideal for stripping leaves and branches from North American forests.
The back of the mouth contained thousands of teeth ideal for grinding food before it was swallowed.
Prosaurolophus had continuously replaced and packed dental batteries containing hundreds of teeth, with only a few active at once.
Prosaurolophus fed on vegetation ranging from the ground up to approximately 4 meters in height.
The crest grew proportionally throughout the animal's life, leading to speculation that it may have supported soft tissue structures like inflatable nasal sacs.
The bony facial crest and possibly nasal diverticula served as potential methods for social display.
Inflatable soft-tissue sacs associated with the crest could have been used for both visual and auditory signals.
Researchers hypothesize that nasal diverticula in Prosaurolophus were soft tissue sacs used for visual and auditory signaling.
Prosaurolophus likely lived in groups for at least part of the year.
Comparisons of scleral rings suggest Prosaurolophus may have been catemeral, active throughout the day with short rest intervals.
Prosaurolophus is classified within the subfamily Saurolophinae.
John Ostrom identified a 'pseudonarial crest' as a unifying feature of Prosaurolophus, Brachylophosaurus, and Saurolophus, distinguishing them from lambeosaurines.
Weishampel and Horner conducted the first cladistic analysis covering Hadrosauridae relationships in 1990.
Prosaurolophus lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 75.7 to 74.1 million years ago.
Prosaurolophus lived during the late Cretaceous, approximately 75 million years ago in the Campanian stage, in what is now North America.
Prosaurolophus maximus was the most common hadrosaurine in the upper section of the Dinosaur Park Formation, deposited about 75.5 million years ago.

The relationship between Prosaurolophus and Saurolophus is debated, with some researchers finding them closely related while others place Prosaurolophus closer to Brachylophosaurus, Edmontosaurus, Gryposaurus, and Maiasaura.
The grouping of Prosaurolophus and Saurolophus has been problematic when trying to place them among hadrosaurines.
Recent studies have considered the differences between the two species insufficient to support them as distinct species.
